title: God From the Machine
gist: This review essay (cut off by a paywall after its opening) frames the pursuit of machine superintelligence as carrying an existential, quasi-religious weight for AI industry leaders — not just a commercial gold rush — and situates a Vatican book on AI ethics (by Pope Leo XIV) as a response to that framing.

themes.theme: Superintelligence as existential, not just commercial, pursuit

insights.claim: The quest for machine superintelligence is not merely a commercial gold rush; for many of its leaders, the prospect carries an existential, tingling significance because of the scale of danger and disruption it promises.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating frontier AI labs should recognize that leadership motivation is partly ideological/existential rather than purely profit-driven, which can affect risk tolerance, safety trade-offs, and capital allocation decisions inside these firms.
insights.quote: The quest for machine superintelligence is not merely a gold rush, motivated by money. In the minds of many of its leaders, the arrival of a new form of cognition has a tingling, existential feel because of the danger and disruption it promises.

insights.claim: The essay frames the emergence of advanced AI as effectively the birth of a new form of cognition — 'a new species' — that outsmarts humans, following billions of years of evolution that produced human intelligence.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: This species-level framing (rather than 'tool' framing) signals how seriously elite commentators are treating the possibility of AI surpassing human cognition, relevant to long-horizon AI-safety and governance debates.
insights.quote: But now we have arrived at a perilous moment—the birth of what amounts to a new species, one that outsmarts humans.

insights.claim: Google executive James Manyika described AI as raising profound existential questions about human identity itself, according to an interview cited in the piece.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Shows that even executives at leading AI developers are publicly framing the technology in existential rather than purely product terms, useful for tracking industry-insider sentiment on AI risk.
